question: How do foundation-model-based multimodal deepfake detectors (vision-language models such as CLIP, vision transformers and self-supervised visual encoders, speech self-supervised encoders, and multimodal LLMs) compare with each other and with conventional CNN-based detectors in reported detection accuracy, cross-dataset and cross-generator generalization, robustness to compression and perturbation, and computational cost, when results are compared only within the same dataset, protocol and metric? Which architectural and adaptation choices (frozen versus fine-tuned backbone, parameter-efficient adaptation, fusion mechanism) are associated with the reported differences?

clarification_answers.What is the primary goal or output of th: A comparative analysis of published results for deepfake detection methods in the provided corpus. The paper is organised around the comparison, not around a taxonomy: define the compared method families and comparison axes, state the comparison protocol, compare methods only within strictly comparable result sets, and end with a decision-oriented synthesis (which family to prefer under which constraint). No experiments were run by the authors: use only results reported in the original studies; never claim to have re-run, re-tuned or re-implemented any model, and never invent, estimate or infer missing numbers.
clarification_answers.Which method families are compared?: (1) Conventional CNN detectors (e.g. Xception, EfficientNet) as the reference family; (2) vision-transformer and self-supervised visual encoders; (3) CLIP and other vision-language models, frozen or adapted (linear probe, prompt tuning, adapters, LoRA, LayerNorm tuning); (4) audio and speech self-supervised encoders (wav2vec 2.0, WavLM, XLS-R); (5) audio-visual fusion detectors; (6) multimodal LLM-based and explainable detectors. Assign each method to a family only as described in its paper; a method may belong to more than one family.
clarification_answers.What makes two results comparable?: Two results are comparable only if they use the same dataset and version (e.g. FaceForensics++ c23, c40 or raw; Celeb-DF v1 or v2; DFDC full or preview), the same train/test protocol (in-domain, cross-dataset with the same training set, cross-generator or cross-manipulation), the same evaluation level (frame-level or video-level) and the same metric and scale (AUC, ACC, EER, AP, F1; ratio or percent). Build one table per comparable setting, with at most 8 columns each. Results from different settings must never be ranked against each other. Mark missing cells as NR, and distinguish Not reported from Not retrieved.
clarification_answers.Which comparison axes should be analyzed: (a) In-domain accuracy; (b) cross-dataset generalization, e.g. trained on FaceForensics++ and tested on Celeb-DF, DFDC or WildDeepfake, reporting the in-domain to cross-dataset drop only when the same source reports both; (c) cross-generator and unseen-manipulation generalization (GAN versus diffusion); (d) robustness to compression, resizing, noise and adversarial perturbation; (e) computational cost (trainable parameters, FLOPs, inference time) only where reported; (f) explainability, as an available capability, not a measured score unless one is reported.
clarification_answers.How should differences between families: Explain observed differences only with design choices that the sources describe (backbone pre-training, frozen versus fine-tuned, adaptation method, fusion location and mechanism, training data). Mark explanations as source-stated or as the authors' interpretation. Do not claim causality from cross-paper comparisons; say when a difference may stem from protocol differences instead of the method.
clarification_answers.What should the conclusion deliver?: A decision-oriented synthesis: for each constraint (cross-dataset generalization, compression robustness, low compute budget, audio-visual input, need for explanations) state which family the comparable evidence favours, how many independent sources support it, and where evidence is missing. Then list the comparison gaps (settings where no comparable results exist) and the experiments that would close them, presented as proposals, not findings.
clarification_answers.What is the intended audience and approx: Researchers in multimedia forensics, computer vision and trustworthy AI. Target an 8-12 page journal manuscript with concise comparison tables, a clearly stated comparison protocol and an explicit limitations section about the fixed 50-paper corpus.
